facts: Trump announced Friday that the U.S. and Russia reached a deal allowing Russian diesel exports to resume, with the U.S. Treasury issuing a temporary license suspending sanctions on those exports until April 7.

Under the announced terms, Russia would release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately, 500,000 tonnes in November, and additional tranches of 1 million and then up to 3 million tonnes depending on the condition of Russian refineries, according to Trump's Truth Social posts.
On Sunday, Trump posted on Truth Social: 'Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed.'

In an ABC 'This Week' interview with Jonathan Karl, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the U.S.-Russia diesel deal a 'birthday gift' to Putin, saying it gives Russia money to continue the war.
Trump said Saturday 'it's time for Ukraine to get a new president' and told reporters Zelensky should stop authorizing Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries.
EU foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas said easing sanctions 'provides Moscow with more revenues to wage war' and said EU foreign ministers planned to approve a new Russia sanctions package on Monday.

Republican Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (Pa.), co-chair of the House Ukraine Caucus, announced Oct. 10 he would introduce the 'Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act' to block Russian oil purchases via a discharge petition, with Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) as co-sponsor.
Russian diesel production has fallen by roughly 30% this year due to Ukrainian drone strikes on refineries, according to International Energy Agency estimates.
ladder.analysis: The dispute sits at the intersection of two Trump administration priorities: lowering U.S. fuel prices before the midterms and brokering an end to the Russia-Ukraine war. Diesel prices have risen sharply in 2025, a problem the White House attributes partly to the ongoing Israel-Iran war's disruption of global oil flows and partly to Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, which have cut Russian diesel output by about a third. The diesel-sanctions deal and the subsequently announced 'energy ceasefire' represent an abrupt reversal from legislation Trump signed in September authorizing tariffs on buyers of Russian energy, and neither Russia nor Ukraine's government has independently confirmed the ceasefire's terms or enforcement mechanism. A similar ceasefire claim made by Trump in September was not confirmed by Moscow and attacks continued, underscoring uncertainty about whether this announcement will hold.
ladder.steelman: Across every outlet, the core tension is that Trump's two biggest claims in this episode — the diesel deal's benefit to U.S. consumers and the existence of an enforceable energy ceasefire — rest almost entirely on his own Truth Social statements, with analysts, Zelensky, and even some congressional Republicans questioning whether either will materially change prices or stop the fighting.
ladder.implications: Whether the diesel deal meaningfully lowers U.S. pump prices, whether Russia and Ukraine actually honor an energy ceasefire, and whether Fitzpatrick's discharge-petition bill or a Democratic joint resolution of disapproval can gather enough votes before the current Congress adjourns in January will determine if this episode becomes a lasting shift in U.S.-Russia sanctions policy or a short-lived, politically motivated announcement ahead of the midterms.

stories.headline: Trump claims Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire; Zelenskyy disputes agreement as strikes continue
stories.byline: International & World desk · anchored on Reuters, AP
body: US President Donald Trump announced Sunday that Ukraine and Russia have agreed to an "energy ceasefire," writing on social media: "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, however, disputed the claim, stating earlier Sunday that Ukraine was "ready to stop striking Russian oil refineries if Russia stops striking our energy infrastructure," and adding that Russia's President Vladimir Putin "does not want to do so."

Trump also intensified his criticism of Zelenskyy, telling reporters at the White House on Saturday: "He better damn well stop" attacking Russian oil refineries, and adding, "I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president." Trump blamed Zelenskyy for rising diesel prices, saying Russia supplies a large portion of global diesel. The comments followed Trump's decision to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian fuel to allow a diesel supply deal with Moscow, a move Zelenskyy warned would embolden Russia. "Today, Russia said thank you for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia," Zelenskyy said Saturday.

Russian attacks on Ukraine continued through the weekend. The State Emergency Service of Ukraine said six people were injured in overnight attacks on four districts in the Dnipropetrovsk region. On Saturday, at least 20 people including four children were killed in Russian attacks on Zaporizhzhia, local officials confirmed. Among the dead was a six-year-old girl whose grandfather, Anatoliy Chumniy, was seen sobbing over her body after rescuers pulled her from rubble. Russia has also struck Ukrainian data centers, causing internet outages and prompting some firms to move servers abroad.

Zelenskyy, who has been pushing for a full ceasefire, told ABC on Sunday that he would organize elections if Putin agrees to a 60-day total ceasefire. "Please tell Putin, give us two months, 60 days of total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organise elections," he said. In response to Trump's suggestion that Ukraine should replace him, Zelenskyy said "it's up to Ukrainians" to choose their leader and noted that Putin would also like to change who is leading Ukraine. The tense relationship between Trump and Zelenskyy extends back to Trump's first term, when he pressured Zelenskyy to investigate Joe Biden and his son Hunter Biden, and has included repeated public rebukes, including Trump calling Zelenskyy a "dictator without elections" in February 2025.

stories.headline: At least 139 dead, 84 missing after migrant boat capsizes off Djibouti
body: At least 139 people, including 15 children, have died and 84 remain missing after a boat carrying more than 300 migrants capsized off the coast of Djibouti, the United Nations migration agency said Sunday. The vessel, which had departed from Djibouti bound for Yemen with an estimated 305 people aboard, went down near the port town of Obock and the Guhere area on Thursday night into Friday, according to survivors cited by the International Organization for Migration (IOM). Around 82 people were rescued, all Ethiopian nationals, as Djiboutian authorities continued search and rescue operations.

The IOM revised its death toll upward from 109 after 30 more bodies were recovered. Of the bodies recovered so far, 52 were men, 42 were women and 15 were children. IOM Djibouti mission chief Alexandre Coissac called the loss of life 'devastating' and said the tragedy was 'a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities.' Local authorities are arranging burials for the dead, while survivors have medical care available and the IOM is providing assistance to 64 of them at its response center in Obock, including healthcare and support to restore contact with their families.

The crossing from Djibouti to Yemen via the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which measures just 20 kilometers (12.4 miles) at its narrowest point, is a popular but perilous route for thousands of migrants from the Horn of Africa. Many undertake the journey driven by poverty, insecurity and the growing impacts of climate change, hoping to reach Gulf countries for safety and work. Since September 10, the IOM said its Displacement Tracking Matrix had observed more than 20,000 movements from Ethiopia to Djibouti. More than 900 migrants died or went missing taking the same route in 2025, during an 18% increase in the number of people attempting the journey, according to IOM statistics.

Yemen remains engulfed in a devastating civil war that has lasted more than a decade, with fighting between Houthi fighters and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government resuming last month. Despite the conflict and growing instability across the wider region, migrants continue to attempt the crossing. The conflict has also displaced more than 130,000 people across Yemen, and thousands of Yemenis have fled to Djibouti to escape the fighting. The IOM urged donors and partners to strengthen support for Djibouti's response, including search and rescue operations and life-saving assistance, and said it was working in close collaboration with local authorities to help migrants and prevent deaths at sea and on land.

stories.headline: India frees 'cockroach' party leaders as protests over voter rolls enter second day
body: New Delhi saw a second consecutive day of sweeping security measures on Sunday as India's Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) pushed ahead with protests demanding the resignation of the country's chief election commissioner, a day after police boarded their flight and detained the movement's founder and two other senior leaders. Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were freed by a magistrate's court after 24 hours in detention on condition that they commit "no breach of peace" for one year. Media reports said about 7,000 protesters were detained and released on Saturday, with hundreds more held on Sunday, in a crackdown that drew a special Supreme Court hearing in which judges called the detentions illegal and ordered the government to restore internet services, allow normal metro and rail operations, permit free movement and end illegal detentions.

The protests centre on a nationwide drive to update electoral rolls that the Election Commission describes as a routine exercise to remove dead, duplicate or ineligible voters but that the CJP and opposition parties say is being manipulated to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). At least 130 million voter names have been purged so far, and tens of thousands of people in many states allege they were wrongly removed; Al Jazeera reported that millions of voters, including Muslims, were deleted in a process marked by technical errors and a perceived lack of transparency. The CJP — which is not registered as a political party — is seeking electoral reforms and has demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar, whom it accuses of disenfranchising voters to help the BJP. The Election Commission and the BJP deny the allegations. An investigation by the Indian Express newspaper found that two of the commission's three members objected to many of Kumar's decisions; the commission is a constitutional body whose decisions are taken by majority.

Saturday's operation turned the capital into a fortress. More than 30,000 police and paramilitary personnel were deployed, according to local media; at least 45 metro stations and Delhi's main railway stations were shut; major train services were cancelled; mobile internet was suspended across several areas; and some protesters travelling from outside the city were de-boarded en route. Authorities refused permission for the planned protest at Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site near parliament, which was sealed off with barricades, concrete blocks and anti-riot vehicles equipped with tear-gas launchers. Police entered an Air India plane after it landed from Mumbai to detain Dipke, Das and Ranka; in a video Dipke shared on Instagram, he told them, "I have come to get arrested. I am not afraid of you guys." Another video showed him saying, "This is dictatorship." Those detained also included YouTuber Dhruv Rathee, All India Students' Association national president Neha Bora, and opposition figures including former chief ministers Mamata Banerjee of West Bengal, Arvind Kejriwal of Delhi and Pinarayi Vijayan of Kerala. About 600 people were arrested in Mumbai, according to the ANI news agency. Small protests elsewhere, including at the Dilli Haat crafts market, were quashed, and journalists from outlets including Scroll.in and Newslaundry were detained, with some reporting that their equipment was seized.

Police said all detainees had been released by Sunday, after the Supreme Court, at a special hearing, called the detentions illegal. In his first comments after his release, Dipke posted on X that "Modi, as PM, is an embarrassment to India. Never has this country seen a bigger coward and bully," and said the CJP "will neither back down nor be intimidated." The leaders accused the Modi government of "waging war" on its own citizens to protect the election commissioner. Das condemned police for "arriving like mafia dons" and "abducting" the group on the plane, and Rathee said he had been "kidnapped." At a news conference, Ranka insisted the bail conditions did not bar further demonstrations. "Peaceful protest is our constitutional right and Jantar Mantar is a designated protest site, so this doesn't mean we can't do peaceful protest," he said. He added: "Breach of peace is done by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Home Minister Amit Shah and CEC Gyanesh Kumar."

The CJP grew out of a post Dipke wrote on X in May — shortly after completing a master's degree at Boston University and having previously worked with the opposition Aam Aadmi Party — asking, "What if all cockroaches come together?" The phrase responded to a remark by Chief Justice Surya Kant likening jobless young people to "cockroaches," which he later said was misinterpreted. The post went viral, and the movement tapped into anger over unemployment, exam paper leaks and government accountability. During five weeks of protests this summer, the group occupied Jantar Mantar to demand education reforms, and its campaign ended in July with the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

On Sunday, much of central Delhi remained barricaded, with offices, shops and restaurants shut and rows of yellow police barriers lining Connaught Place, one of the city's busiest commercial hubs. The BBC witnessed protesters being chased, detained and bundled into buses as small groups slipped past barricades chanting "Gyanesh must go!" Some demonstrators acknowledged the impact of the leadership's absence. "Without them, we're feeling a little lost," one protester told the BBC, "but that doesn't mean we'll stop our fight." With crucial state elections just months away, the CJP and student groups said protests would continue despite the detentions, and leaders vowed they would neither back down nor be intimidated.

stories.headline: Wall Street Kicks Off Q3 Earnings Season With Bank Results, High Expectations
body: The third-quarter earnings season begins this week, led by the largest U.S. banks, as investors gauge whether corporate profits can sustain the stock market's momentum amid rising Treasury yields and elevated oil prices. Analysts forecast that earnings among S&P 500 companies will rise approximately 31% year over year, with technology and AI-related businesses accounting for roughly two-thirds of the increase, according to LSEG estimates. The S&P 500 climbed to an all-time high last week, but the benchmark has been volatile recently due to concerns that the Federal Reserve may raise rates further to curb inflation.

JPMorgan Chase, Goldman Sachs, Citigroup and Wells Fargo are scheduled to report results on Tuesday, followed by Morgan Stanley and Bank of America on Wednesday. Overall, 25 S&P 500 companies are set to release quarterly figures this week. JPMorgan is expected to report double-digit earnings growth from a year earlier, after posting a 41% year-on-year earnings jump last quarter. Goldman Sachs' top and bottom lines are forecast to have grown 10% and around 6%, respectively. Citigroup is expected to report sharp year-on-year earnings growth, while Wells Fargo is forecast to post earnings growth of more than 10%, per LSEG data. Morgan Stanley's top line is expected to have grown nearly 10%, and Bank of America is expected to report single-digit year-on-year earnings and revenue growth.

The results come at a delicate time for the financial sector. Over the past month, the Financial Services sector was the second-worst performing sector in the S&P 500, losing roughly 4%. As of Friday's market close, the five major banks have lost roughly $270 billion in market capitalization. Only 35% of institutional investors expect bank stocks to outperform the broader market, down from 68% in July and 82% in December, per a Truist Securities study. Wells Fargo shares are down 13% over the past month, the most among six major U.S. banks.

Analysts are watching for how banks discuss the impact of higher interest rates. Seaport Research Partners said of JPMorgan: "While we raised our [net interest income] forecast for next year on the higher forward curve ... we are above consensus on expenses, which could be guided higher as well." TD Cowen initiated Goldman Sachs as a buy, stating: "GS is leveraging its enormous scale to benefit from the favorable capital markets and asset-price backdrops." Jefferies analyst David Chiaverini has a buy rating on Citigroup, citing its "improving return profile." Barclays has an overweight rating on Bank of America, though analyst Jason Goldberg expects "somewhat mixed results."

Beyond banks, investors will also get results from UnitedHealth and Johnson & Johnson, providing a view on the healthcare sector, and from ASML and Taiwan Semiconductor, offering checks on the AI trade. On the economic data front, Wednesday's consumer inflation report is expected to be a major factor for the Federal Reserve's rate decision at its October meeting. The wholesale inflation check via the Producer Price Index is due Thursday, along with readings on industrial production and manufacturing activity on Friday.

The broader earnings picture shows growth moderating from the second quarter, when S&P 500 earnings increased nearly 54% year over year, the highest rate since 2021. Energy sector earnings are projected to rise approximately 115% year over year, following a roughly 30% increase in U.S. crude oil prices during the quarter amid the ongoing U.S.-Israeli conflict with Iran. Consumer staples and real estate are among the sectors with the lowest expected year-over-year earnings growth. Sameer Samana, head of global equities and real assets at Wells Fargo Investment Institute, said: "It's all AI and, to a lesser extent, energy and materials, but that's because of geopolitics. It wouldn't surprise me if 70-80% of the growth can be attributed to tech and AI."

stories.headline: Princeton lab finds potentially more efficient route to fusion energy
body: Scientists at the U.S. Department of Energy's Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL) have identified a potentially far more efficient path to fusion ignition, according to calculations published in the journal Physical Review Letters. The approach reverses the traditional sequence: instead of first increasing plasma density and then applying enormous heat, the researchers propose heating the plasma before making it denser. Their generalized version of the Lawson criterion — the mathematical rule that for more than seven decades has defined the conditions needed for a self-sustaining fusion reaction — incorporates four additional factors that can dramatically alter the energy required to reach ignition.

The new model, developed by PPPL physicists Luis Delgado-Aparicio, Masayuki Ono, and Jonathan Menard, maps a route that avoids the highest energy demands. Delgado-Aparicio compared the discovery to finding a smarter way through a mountain range: “A lot of companies want to climb the mountain head-on and spend enormous energy to get there. Go around the peak instead. You reach the same place in a much smarter way, and you use far less energy.” The key region in this mathematical landscape is the Cordey saddle, a relatively accessible point along the boundary between plasma that still requires external heating and plasma capable of sustaining its own fusion reactions. In an idealized plasma containing only pure fusion fuel, the Cordey saddle occurs at a Q value of about 5 — where Q compares the power produced by fusion reactions with the external heating power supplied. However, contaminants and strong magnetic fields can shift this passage, raising the Q needed.

The researchers incorporated four physical processes that previous work often examined separately: helium ash buildup from fusion reactions, plasma contamination from light and heavy impurities, synchrotron radiation emitted by electrons in magnetic fields, and continuous heat loss from the plasma. “When you leave these effects out, you say the design will work fine,” Ono said. “When you put them in, the picture changes, and it becomes quite important.” One striking finding concerns tungsten, a heat-resistant metal selected for the interior walls of more than a dozen next-generation fusion machines. The team's calculations show that tungsten contamination at a concentration of just one part in 10,000 can approximately double the pressure required to achieve fusion ignition. When the analysis was extended to three dimensions, the pressure needed could exceed the limits at which the plasma remains stable.

The findings could influence the design of tokamaks and stellarators, two major types of magnetic fusion devices that use powerful magnetic fields to confine plasma while it is heated to temperatures greater than those at the center of the sun. The study also identifies technologies that might help overcome the obstacles revealed by the calculations, including liquid lithium coatings that could prevent tungsten from entering the plasma and reduce heat losses, as well as spin-polarized fuel that could increase the fusion reaction rate. Surprisingly, some of the energy losses that make ignition more difficult may also help stabilize a burning plasma by counteracting thermal runaway, a self-reinforcing cycle of heat and reaction rate that could otherwise become unstable.

The proposed heat-first approach has not yet been demonstrated experimentally; the research is theoretical and relies on mathematical calculations. Existing fusion experiments have not reached the temperatures associated with the Cordey saddle, preventing direct testing. The PPPL team plans to investigate the approach further through computer-based simulations. “While more study is needed, we are excited by these results, and they suggest a clear path forward for future research in this area,” said Menard. The work was supported by the DOE Office of Science, Office of Fusion Energy Sciences, under contract DE-AC02-09CH11466, with additional support from a 2015 Fusion Energy Sciences Early Career Award, a 2018 Diagnostic Innovation and Development award, and the 2021 and 2025 Long-Pulse Tokamak Research Programs.
